sections.body: The Art of AI covers ten creative disciplines where artificial intelligence is used to make or alter work. In visual arts, systems generate images from text prompts and assist with inpainting and style transfer. In video, models synthesize short clips and help with rotoscoping and frame interpolation. In music, tools separate stems, generate melodies, and clone voices for operatic or studio use. In dance, motion capture data is mapped to new bodies or choreographic sequences. In writing, language models draft passages, suggest plot turns, and imitate authorial voice. In theater, AI helps design virtual sets and lighting cues. In photography, generative fill and upscaling create hyper-real images that may never have been shot. In interactive art, models respond to visitors in real time. Across all of this, the actual work is often a loop of human direction, machine output, and manual correction.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Image generation is the most mature, with widely used tools that produce coherent stills, but hands, text, and fine detail still fail often. Video synthesis is less stable, with short clips and flicker or morphing artifacts. Audio and music tools can produce convincing short phrases, but long-form structure and emotional arc remain weak. Vocal synthesis can clone a voice from a few minutes of audio, yet expressive control is limited. Choreography and motion mapping work well for abstract movement but struggle with contact and weight. Literary tools are fluent but shallow, often repeating clichés and losing track of facts. Theater and virtual set design are promising but require heavy manual cleanup. Photography and hyper-realism raise the hardest question: what counts as a photograph. Interactive art is experimental and often breaks. The honest limit is that no listed discipline has a fully autonomous creative system; every output needs human selection, editing, or correction. The atlas currently tracks no live image, video, or audio models and no active intellectual property lawsuits, so these pages describe the field without a running count of tools.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader interested in still images should start with Visual Arts and Generative Illustration, then move to Photography and Hyper-Realism to see how the same techniques blur documentary truth. For moving images, Cinematography and Video Synthesis pairs with Choreography and Motion Mapping, since both rely on frame prediction and pose estimation. For sound, Vocal Synthesis and Operatic Performance and Music Composition and Audio Engineering cover the voice and the mix separately, but they share stem separation and timbre transfer. Literary Arts and Narrative Design stands alone for text, while Theater and Virtual Set Design connects writing, image, and motion in a physical space. Interactive and Experiential Art is the most cross-disciplinary page, pulling from all of the above. Rights and Provenance in AI Art should be read last, because it addresses ownership, attribution, and the legal status of everything described in the other nine pages.
